The present perfect and the past simple are verb tenses you use to talk about past events. Let's see how they are different.

The present perfect is used to talk about actions that started in the past and continue to the present. Also, to talk about an action that started in the past and whose consequence is still visible in the present. The time the action happened is unstated since it is not relevant in the context. To form the present perfect, we need the auxiliary have/ has and the past participle of the main verb. Have a look at this structure:

Subject + have/has+ verb past participle+ complement

For example:

I have worked with Java for 3 years. (The exact time I started to work with Java is not important, so it is not stated. Moreover, the action is still visible in the present since I’m still working with it. )

The past simple, for its part, is used to describe an event that started in the past and finished in the past. Besides, the time it happened is important in the context, so, different from the present perfect, the time is stated. Look at the structure:

Subject+ verb in past form+ complement.

For example:

I started to work with Java in 2008. (Note that the time is stated.)

Yesterday, the teacher explained how to use comments when working with Java.  (The action started yesterday and finished yesterday.)

Java comments are statements or notes that are included in the Java code. The compiler and the runtime engine don't execute the comments since they are only there to provide information or to explain something about the variable, class or method in which they are included.

Java supports 3 types of comments: Single Line Comment, Multi Line Comment and Documentation Comment.

Single Line Comment

To make use of a single line comment, start typing two forward slashes (//) and then your comment:

 // this is my comment

 The compiler identifies immediately that all the information next to theses slashes is a comment.

Multi Line Comment

This is also known as a traditional comment. To make use of it, write your comment enclosing it between (/*) and (*/): 

(/*) This is my very first
comment (*/)

As you can see, this type of comment is used when the information you want to enter does not meet the requirement of a single line.

Documentation Comments

You use this kind of comment to document when you want to document the API of the code you’re forming. In order to accomplish this, you’ll need to use the Javadoc tool. Put the comment between ( /**) and (*/):

/**  * This is my
* comment. */

Teacher: Good morning, everyone. Today, we’ll go back over what we’ve studied these days on Java. Yesterday, we read about commenting. So, Sara, what can you tell me about it?
Sara: Well, I’ve done some research, and I’ve written a short text in order to organize the information I found.
Teacher: Good! Go ahead, read your text.

Sara: “Commenting is an essential component in any programming task since it helps the programmer or the one who is reading the code to fully comprehend the function of that code inside the program, not to mention the amount of time you can save by using it. These comments or notes, which are included in a Java code file, are always overlooked by the compiler and the runtime engine, so they do not affect how the program runs. One of the advantages of commenting in Java is that we can add an unlimited number of comments, so we don’t need to restrict the notes. However, to do it properly, we’ve got to know certain rules and types of comments that will let us organize the information, so we can better the readability of the code. First, we should know that Java supports three types of comments: Single Line Comment, Multi Line Comment, and Documentation Comment. Each one of these comments allows you to add your comments based on their length and intention. Single line comments, for example, are known as the simplest ones since they are used to add information that does not extend one single line. Start typing two forward slashes (//) and then your comment. Remember that you can also form nested comments, which are single line comments that are included in a block of code. The multi-line comments, also known as the traditional comments, go beyond one single line. To make use of them, enclose your comment between (/*) and (*/). Finally, there are documentation comments, or doc comments, which are used to document the API of the code you’re writing. To use them you should know how to use the Javadoc tool. They are very similar to the multi-line comments, but you have to place your comment between ( /**) and (*/).”

Teacher: Well done! I’d like to complement what you’ve said with some tips we reviewed the class you didn’t come. First, avoid getting used to over commenting. Although comments are extremely useful, you don’t need to fill the code up with them; it should flow logically without the need of a great number of comments. Second, add your comments while you’re working on your source code. If you add them later, you may have lots of problems. Finally, don’t forget to modify and update your comments as you move forward!
